n: Written by John Taylor, an eyewitness, this section announces the martyrdom of Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum on June 27, 1844, at Carthage Jail, Illinois. A mob of 150–200 men with blackened faces attacked; both brothers were killed.

f.g: The attackers darkened their faces with mud and gunpowder to hide their identities.
Joseph’s final words as he fell from the window.

n: John Taylor and Willard Richards were also in the room. Taylor was badly wounded; Richards escaped virtually unharmed, fulfilling an earlier prophecy by Joseph.

f.w: without even a hole in his robe
f.g: Joseph had reportedly prophesied that Willard Richards would escape unharmed.

n: John Taylor testifies that, apart from Jesus, Joseph did more for human salvation than anyone else. In about twenty years he brought forth the Book of Mormon, sent the gospel worldwide, received the revelations, gathered thousands, and founded Nauvoo. He and Hyrum were united in life and in death.

f.w: translated by the gift and power of God
In life they were not divided, and in death they were not separated
a fame and name that cannot be slain

n: Days before, Joseph said he was going “like a lamb to the slaughter,” yet calm, with a clear conscience. That morning Hyrum read from Ether 12 and folded down the page.

f.w: like a lamb to the slaughter

n: The passage Hyrum marked: Moroni’s words that even if others lack charity, the faithful will be made clean and strong, and will meet them at the judgment seat. Taylor adds Paul’s idea that a testament takes effect when the testator dies.

f.w: The testators are now dead, and their testament is in force

n: Hyrum was 44, Joseph 38. Their sacrifice shows the cost of bringing forth these books. If the “green tree” is burned, how much more the dry—Jesus’ warning on the way to the cross.

f.w: if the fire can scathe a green tree

n: They were innocent, jailed through conspiracy despite the governor’s pledge of protection. Their blood is a seal on their testimony and joins the martyrs under the altar crying for justice.

f.g: A shield bearing a coat of arms; here, the reputation or honor of the state.
The Magna Carta of 1215, symbol of legal rights; here, the U.S. Constitution.

f.w: the martyrs under the altar that John saw
